伊東甲子太郎.note: Born Suzuki Daizō in Hitachi; a Hokushin Ittō-ryū adept and Mito-school loyalist ideologue who kept a dōjō at Fukagawa in Edo. He joined the Shinsengumi at the end of 1864, meaning all along to turn it into a topple-the-shogunate party. His faction would later break away as the Kōdai-ji guardsmen and be destroyed.

尾形俊太郎.note: A jokin of the Shinsengumi and one of its few lettered men, employed by Kondō on documentary and liaison work.

鈴木三樹三郎.note: Itō Kashitarō's younger brother, who joined the corps with him. He later broke away with the Kōdai-ji faction, survived the Restoration, and lived to old age.

ch26.note: Itō Kashitarō (1835–1867) is the figure whose coming reshapes the middle of the book. A polished swordsman and a fluent theorist of the revere-the-Emperor, topple-the-shogunate school, he enters the Shinsengumi meaning to capture it from within — the design he lays out to Tōdō in this chapter. Three years on, the split he seeds here will end at the Aburanokōji: Kondō will have him killed and use his corpse to bait and cut down his followers.

ch26.anchor: the kinoe-ne of the first year of Genji
ch26.note: In the old sexagenary calendar every year bears one of sixty combined signs; kinoe-ne (甲子) is the first of the sixty, a year reckoned auspicious for new beginnings. Its two characters can be read kasshi as well, and from them the man took his new name, Kashitarō — announcing, in effect, a fresh start. The first year of Genji was 1864.

The Hokushin Ittō-ryū, founded by Chiba Shūsaku (1793–1856) at his Genbukan dōjō at Otamagaike in Kanda, was one of the three great fencing schools of late-Tokugawa Edo. Patronized by the loyalist Mito house, it turned out an extraordinary run of revolutionary swordsmen — Kiyokawa Hachirō, Sakamoto Ryōma, and others — which is precisely the political taint Toshizō smells on it.

Kinchō: a warrior sealed an inviolable promise by striking steel on steel — the guard of his own sword, or two blades together — so that the ring of the metal stood witness to the oath. Here Itō pledges to keep Tōdō’s murderous secret, without yet pledging the deed.

Takeda Kōunsai (1803–1865), an elder councillor of the Mito domain and leader of its radical loyalists. In 1864 he headed the armed rising of the Tengu Party (the “Tengu-tō”); it was crushed, and he was executed. That Itō stood close to such a man marks how far his own loyalism ran.
